coach_says: Your d5 pawn was doing an important job: it defended e4 and kept the d-file closed. After dxc4 bxc4 your knight on b5 is attacked again anyway, the d-file opens for White's rook, and the e4 pawn is left on its own for the knight on c5 to pick off. Instead, retreat the knight first with Nc7, where it also watches a6 and a8 against White's passed pawn, and keep your d5-e4 chain intact.

White's king is still on e1 and your knight on c6 is already hitting d4, so this is the moment to strike in the centre with ...e5. That opens lines towards the uncastled king and gets your pieces into play with gain of time. Bd7 is a quiet developing move that lets White play a3 and castle in peace; when the enemy king is still in the middle, look for the pawn break that opens the centre.

You are behind in development: your d-pawn, c8 bishop and b8 knight have not moved and your king is in the centre. ...d5 attacks the queen and frees your bishop at the same time, so it develops with tempo. b5 also hits the queen, but it develops nothing and leaves a loose pawn on b5 and a weak c6 that White's pieces can target later (Qc3, Bxb5).

g4 puts a pawn on a square nothing of yours defends. As soon as Black plays ...d5 the c8 bishop sees g4 and simply takes it. Before pushing a pawn forward, check who protects it on its new square; here g3 and a fianchettoed bishop would have done the same job safely.

The pawn on d5 was the only thing blocking White's queen from your bishop on d7. When you took on c4 you opened the d-file and White answered Qxd7, so the bishop you won came straight back and your queen is now facing an active queen with weak, split c-pawns. Before capturing with a pawn, ask what that pawn was shielding; here Qb7 or Qa5, getting your pieces active first, kept you in the game.

c6 is a reasonable way to challenge White's d5 pawn and the engine barely separates it from the alternatives. Just remember f6 has already loosened your kingside, so getting the king safe with moves like g6, Bh6 or Ne7 soon is important.
Castling here is a sound, natural move and costs very little. Bb3 to keep the bishop away from ...b5 hits was slightly more precise, but there is nothing important to change.

Well found. c3 attacks the checking bishop, and because your bishop on b5 pins the d7 knight, Black can't easily keep everything defended; you come out with extra material. This was the best move by a distance.
Good choice. Taking the knight on b3 removes a defender and keeps your winning endgame simple, and it is the engine's top move. Keep trading down into a won ending like this.

You are already a lot of material down after the earlier sacrifice, and Bd6 is about as good as anything here; the small difference is not something to worry about. Focus on activating your pieces and keeping your king safe.
Recapturing with the knight is fine and you keep a strong position with your extra material. Kxe7 was marginally better, but both recaptures do the job.

Qd5 is one of several equal moves in a difficult position where you are a piece for two pawns down. There is no specific improvement to learn here; keep your queen active and try to make the passed c-pawns count.
e4 is a reasonable move, gaining space and fixing the centre, and it is almost as good as the engine's Nf5. Nothing important to change here.
Ne5 is a normal plan against this Stonewall-style setup and costs very little. c4 to challenge d5 straight away is slightly more principled, but this is fine.

Nh2 takes a well-placed knight back to the edge and does nothing; Black is no worse off than if you had passed. Black's queen on g6 is exposed, so this was the time to act: d4 strikes the centre while Black's king is still on e8, and h5 kicks the queen with tempo. Avoid undeveloping moves in the opening unless there is a concrete reason.

You have given up a rook for an attack, so you need open lines and you need to keep queens on. Qf3+ lets the king step back to e8, and then exd5 Qxd5 offers a queen trade, and ...dxe4 can hit your queen. Playing exd5 first opens the e-file and diagonals while Black's king is still exposed, and Qf3+ can come after.

The e5 pawn was attacked twice, by your knight on f3 and your rook on e1, and only defended once, by the knight on c6, because Black's own bishop on e6 blocks the queen. Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 wins a pawn and leaves Black tied up by the pin on f6 and the pressure on e6. Count attackers and defenders on every enemy pawn before making a quiet move like b3.

White's b4 did more than push a pawn: it cleared the second rank, so the queen on f2 now attacks your bishop on a2, and nothing defends it. After Rbc8 White simply plays Qxa2 with check. When your opponent moves a pawn or piece, look at what lines it opens; here Be6 or Bf7 brings the bishop back to safety.
concept: discovered attack on the a2 bishop

coach_says: Your knight on d4 was attacked by the rook on d1 and nothing defended it, so Rfc8 just loses it to Rxd4. Before every move, check which of your pieces are under attack. Ne2+ saves the knight with check, and after Kh1 you take on a3 with a big advantage.

Your bishop was attacked by ...axb5, but before retreating look for checks: Qe6+ forces ...Qe7, and then Bxd7+ cashes in on the pinned knight. Bc4 also steps away from d7 and does nothing about Black's bishop on the long diagonal, which now takes on b2 and goes after your rook on a1. When a piece is attacked, look first for a forcing move that keeps the initiative.
